newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's new army chief - experience with rebellions.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's new army chief - experience with rebellions.

text.p: General Mahele Lieko Bokoungo, Zaire's new army chief, has popped up on repeated occasions since President Mobutu Sese Seko seized power in 1965 to help quell internal rebellions.

An experienced and respected officer trained in France and Israel and by Zaire's former colonial rulers Belgium, he has been granted unprecedented powers to control the hitherto untouchable presidential guard.
Mobutu returned from a prolonged absence in Europe on Tuesday and the next day named Mahele to take command of the Zairean Armed Forces, who have been sent reeling by a Tutsi-led revolt in the east.

Mobutu fired Mahele from the same post in 1993 and military sources say the general gave stiff conditions before accepting to resume army command. These include powers to sanction senior officers and total control over the armed forces including the elite presidential guard, until now answerable to Mobutu alone.

The sources indicated that his request to control the entire armed forces had been accepted, and that he would now be charged with re-uniting the divided sections of the military in order to drive back the rebel invasion in the east.
Before his appointment, political leaders, local newspapers and regular soldiers battling Rwandan-backed ethnic Tutsis all called for him to take command.
Some sources say Mahele has the blessing of France, which has troops stationed in Africa and intervened in the past to help Mobutu.

Mahele is respected among rank and file soldiers and has a reputation for discipline and military skill among the wider population, making him the obvious choice to boost troop morale and restore public confidence in the ragged Zairean army.
Mahele is one of the rare top generals in Zaire who have earned their senior ranking position on the battlefield and not through close family ties with Mobutu.
Born in 1941, Mahele was recruited into the army the year Mobutu took over power in a military coup d'etat, in 1965.
"Mahele is a trained carpenter who became a fervent Jehovah's Witness, going from door to door to spread his message," one Zaire watcher wrote in 1991.
He is from the Mbuza tribe which is close to Mobutu's Gbandi. On many occasions in Zaire's turbulent post-independence history, he has played a role in suppressing internal rebellion.

He was Mobutu's chief bodyguard for several years from 1969. Unlike other top generals, he is not from Mobutu's direct clan or family, and has avoided a reputation for corruption or lavish living that some of Mobutu's closer generals have attracted.

Eleven years ago he fought back Laurent Kabila, who had set up a rebel republic on the shores of Lake Tanganyika around the town of Moba. Kabila heads the rebel alliance which has seized border towns and territory since fighting erupted on October 18.

Mahele's role will be to restore order among mutinous troops who have fled the fighting in the east leaving a trail of destruction and pillage in their wake, before attempting a counter-offensive to recapture rebel-held territory.

He also had experience fighting Tutsi rebels in Rwanda when he led Zairean soldiers in 1990 to back up the Hutu regime of the late president Juvenal Habyarimana. But the Tutsi rebels went on to seize power in 1994 and are supporting the present revolt in eastern Zaire.

In 1991 Mahele rose to the position of chief of staff of the armed forces and was widely credited with putting down a round of army-led looting in the capital Kinshasa when he gave orders for loyal troops to fire on looters in 1993.
But when he criticised the army's role in Zaire before a national conference that year, and called for reforms, he was removed from the position.
Since then he has kept a low profile as military adviser to the president.
